claims.text: A multiscale framework combining ab initio electron-phonon calculations with defect-sensitive lattice dynamics can separately predict phonon and electronic thermal conductivity in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed framework will improve predictive accuracy by roughly 20% relative to Debye-based and ideal-crystal DFT approaches.
HfNbTaTiZr is considered in a concentrated, single-phase refractory high-entropy-alloy state.
The relevant HfNbTaTiZr samples include defect-minimized material and material containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The proposed method explicitly integrates electronic structure, phonon dispersion, electron-phonon coupling, and impurity or defect scattering.
Below 200 K, lattice and electronic thermal-conductivity contributions in HfNbTaTiZr are comparable.
Oxygen-containing HfNbTaTiZr has been experimentally studied from 300 to 1200 K.
Random solid-solution high-entropy alloys exhibit local lattice distortions caused by atomic-size mismatch.
HfNbTaTiZr specifically exhibits random lattice distortions that must be modeled for thermal transport.
Random alloy environments can produce substantial local variations in interatomic force constants.
Oxygen impurities significantly alter scattering and thermal transport in HfNbTaTiZr.
Accounting for impurity-induced scattering, lattice distortions, and force-constant variations remedies complexities neglected by Debye-based and standard DFT simulations.
Decoupling lattice vibrations from electronic excitations will improve the accuracy of the predicted thermal-conductivity components.
Each predicted component, phonon and electronic thermal conductivity, will lie within ±20% of its experimentally determined value.
The model will reproduce comparable phonon and electronic contributions below 200 K.
For oxygen-containing samples at high temperature, the model will reproduce a total thermal conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m).
Existing Debye and DFT-derived elastic-property approaches assume perfect defect-free crystals and conflate lattice and electronic conductivity.
The proposed framework is applicable to HfNbTaTiZr from approximately 50 to 1200 K, provided impurity levels and chemical inhomogeneity do not greatly exceed the modeled level.
The Wiedemann-Franz law provides only a coarse estimate of electronic thermal conductivity and can yield nonphysical results in some alloys.
Uncertainty in experimentally separating electronic and lattice conductivity may limit direct validation of the framework.
